title: Kernel handoffs and stall transitions: profiling notes
content:
Purpose
Quick working notes from a short investigation into sudden latency spikes that correlate with attention kernel switches (FlashAttention <-> paged attention) and moments where fused ops unexpectedly serialize. Goal is to capture hypotheses, quick reproducer configs, initial traces, and next experiments. This is a working doc — rough, partial, and intentionally experimental.

Background / why this matters
- Production QA traces show ~95th/99th token-latency spikes for mixed-length workloads that we suspect are related to kernel handoffs.
- Our runtime can select different attention implementations (fast fused Flash style kernels for short-to-medium sequences vs paged/flash-paged for long sequences). Switching between implementations mid-stream or between adjacent requests appears to create transient stalls or queueing.

Short summary of observed symptoms
- Tail latency spikes aligned to boundaries where model sequence length for a request crosses a threshold (e.g., 512 -> 520 tokens bracket).
- Nsight timeline shows short (~100-400us) idle gaps on the stream during which the device is under-utilized, followed by bursted kernel launches and higher SM utilization.
- When fused ops are enabled, the handoff sometimes causes a ~2–3x increase in kernel launch count for the same logical token processing step.
- On small-batch, single-request workloads we still see kernel-launch overhead dominating when the pipeline chooses a different kernel variant than the last request.

Test harness and config used so far
- Model: distilled transformer (3B-ish) served in local dev cluster (A100s).
- Workload generator: synthetic request stream with Zipf-ish seq length mix: 30% <=256, 50% 257-512, 20% 513-1536. Interarrival: Poisson with mean 5ms.
- Runtime flags: "auto-select-kernel=on", "fusion=enabled", "kv-prefetch=on". Also exercised fusion=off and kv-prefetch=off.
- Profiling: Nsight Systems capture (timeline + API events), CUDA kernel timestamps via CUPTI lightweight counters, and custom event traces (request begin/step/token).

Key trace snippets (high level)
- Timeline example A: Request A (seq 480) processed with Flash kernel variant. Immediately after, Request B (seq 520) arrives; runtime schedules paged attention kernels. Timeline shows: 190us gap (no device work), then three small copy+kernels back-to-back. Request B token latency 450us vs expected 200us.
- Timeline example B: Same request order but with fusion disabled — latency regresses by 20%, but the idle gap length shortens.

Immediate hypotheses
1) Kernel selection switching causes resource reconfiguration overhead (different kernel grid/block sizes, shared-memory or scratchpad allocation patterns, and different stream priorities) leading to stalls while the runtime serializes setup operations.
2) CUDA kernel launch serialization due to stream synchronization: we have a mix of streams (compute, prefetch/copy) and some ops implicitly synchronize when switching between fused and paged paths.
3) Memory allocator fragmentation / GC during kernel swap: new kernel variant requires temporary buffers or different allocation patterns; allocator path triggers slow path and causes a pause.
4) Kernel-thin microkernels (helper fused ops) produce many more launches for paged path -> overhead amortization is worse for small seqs.
5) Device-side occupancy ramp-up: some kernels require more SMs or different occupancy; switching causes short epochs of masked threads while caches warm -> briefly low throughput.

Quick checks run and results
- Disable auto kernel switch: forcing paged-only removes the gap but average latency increases for shorter sequences. So switching logic contributes but is not the only issue.
- Pre-warm both kernel variants at worker startup (launch a dummy dispatch) reduces the idle gap by ~40% in initial reproducer — suggests some warmup / JIT / driver warming effects.
- Use of CUDA graphs to capture both variants and replay reduces per-request overhead substantially, but integration complexity high and interaction with dynamic seq lengths remains an open question.
- Replacing custom allocator with cudaMalloc/free shows longer pauses, so allocator isn't the sole culprit; our pooled allocator reduces worst-case overhead.
- Changing stream model (all compute on single high-priority stream) eliminated serialization artifacts in one experiment but increased contention and occasional priority inversion for copy ops.

Measurements and metrics (representative numbers)
- Kernel-launch overhead (measured delta from enqueue to start): 25–300us depending on kernel size and recent history.
- Idle-gap measured between last kernel of Request A and first kernel of Request B: 80–420us (median ~170us in mixed workload).
- Increase in kernel launches when using fused ops + paged path: +2 to +6 small launches per token step in some code paths.
- SM utilization drop during gap: from avg 70% -> 8% during stall window.

Potential mitigations (ranked quick list)
- Pre-warm both kernel variants at worker start and periodically when idle (cheap, reproducible benefit).
- Batch alignment heuristics: pad or split sequences to avoid frequent variant flipping at token boundaries. Example: coerce short requests to round-up length to nearest variant bucket when latency tradeoff acceptable.
- Persistent kernels / kernel residency: attempt to retain key kernel modules resident via dummy periodic dispatch or use of CUDA graphs to avoid JIT/driver handshake.
- Consolidate streams: move to single compute stream for main kernel dispatch to avoid implicit cross-stream syncs (beware copy priority tradeoffs).
- Reduce microkernel count in paged path: combine small helper kernels where possible to amortize launch overhead.
- Scheduler-level smoothing: delay dispatch of a borderline request by <1ms to allow coalescing with following similar-length requests (trade latency for tail reduction).
- Explicit allocator optimizations: ensure per-stream or per-kernel buffer pools with fixed-size slabs to avoid allocator slow paths when swapping variants.

Planned follow-ups / experiments (short-term runbook)
1) Synthetic microbench matrix: systematically vary (seq-length, batch-size, fusion on/off, prefetch on/off) and measure idle-gap, kernel-launch counts, and token P50/P99. Produce a heatmap. (Owner: Diego)
2) Nsight capture suite: capture worst-case and median traces for both A100 and H100 to check device/driver differences. (Owner: Priya)
3) Scoped change: implement periodic pre-warm dispatch for current canary image and measure tail-latency change over 48h (Owner: Ava).
4) Kernel consolidation PR: prototype combining 2–3 helper ops in paged path to reduce launches; microbench against fusion disabled to validate. (Owner: Ethan)
5) Add telemetry: instrument runtime to emit kernel-variant decisions and per-request kernel counts to tracing pipeline; create alert if kernel-handoff gap > 200us at >1% of requests. (Owner: Ava)

Open questions / unknowns
- Do certain sequence content characteristics (e.g., attention sparsity or kv-cache size) affect the selection logic beyond raw length? We need to probe model-internal triggers.
- Interaction with other tenants on the GPU (multi-tenant servers) — does other process activity amplify the gap due to L2 eviction or SM scheduling?
- Impact of driver version / CUDA runtime: preliminary check between 11.8 and 12.x shows marginal differences; need broader sweep.

Notes to self / TODO snippets
- Add a quick script to spawn two interleaved request workloads with deterministic timing (reproducer_agent.py) and attach Nsight automatically.
- Confirm whether kernel modules get recompiled at runtime under specific model variants — check loader output / JIT logs.
- Run experiment reducing the dispatch priority difference instead of collapsing streams.

Relevant logs / commands used
- nsight-sys --trace=cuda --output=trace-512-520.nsys --duration=30s --target-pid=<server-pid>
- CUPTI lightweight kernel timestamps exported to /tmp/trace-kernel-ts.csv
- runtime flags: --kernel-selection-policy=auto --fusion=true --kv-prefetch=true

Concluding thoughts
This looks like a combination of kernel selection overhead + launch-amortization issues for microkernels. The good news: pre-warm and kernel consolidation experiments show tangible wins; they are low-risk changes we can test in canary. Longer-term, we should aim to reduce variant churn (selection hysteresis), consolidate helper kernels in the paged path, and improve telemetry so we can target exact request signatures that flip variants.

If you're poking at this doc: please add any extra traces or weird reproducer cases below.

-- Ava
